I'm of the opinion autism is just the population adjusting to a different way of thinking.

I'm of the opinion that autism is just the ordinary expression of genetic factors that's a normal part of human brain evolution. Then again, I'm actually autistic and can directly experience the fundamental differences between myself and everyone else as opposed to just making things up through my ignorance of the situation. Aside from that, there's a problem with overdiagnosis and inadequate standards to determine whether or not someone's autistic. I've seen more than a few people "diagnosed" as adults that don't seem even slightly autistic.

So the point of this is we don't know what is causing it to go up, correlation is not causation, so there will not be 50% by 2025. But isn't there an increase? Shouldn't we try and figure out what is causing it instead of arguing about the future that we could change?

The growth in autism rates? I'm gonna go with overdiagnosis. Autism became popular for some reason and gets overdiagnosed just like ADD and a host of other real problems. It gets to a point where people start doubting anyone has a legit diagnosis because they keep coming across erroneous cases.

I can't even begin to tell you the number of times where people have looked at the symptoms and said "that kinda describes me too!" when it really, really doesn't. Not even a little bit. There was a rash of articles in the early-to-mid 2000s about how these famous tech people have Asperger's or how these well-known historical figures do - never with a proper diagnostic setting, mind you; even the living people had pure speculation given - which basically went out of their way to make it as some sort of boon to their success(left out, of course, were the major negatives that make it a syndrome in the first place). Self-diagnosis started becoming popular about then(first among internet assholes, then moving over to special snowflakes), which wouldn't affect numbers, but those articles probably biased parents into bringing their children in at much higher rates simply looking to see if their child was headed for "success"; given that diagnosis of any mental disorder is more an art than a science, there are probably plenty of odd-but-normal people out there who were misdiagnosed simply because the psychiatrist expected there to be a good reason for the referral.

Windows applications removing the menu bar ala Office Suite style.

The general trend of removing the menu bar has been going on progressively for the past several years, thanks in part to decisions made by Microsoft, Apple, and Google (via Chrome) among other software makers, along with the general trend to try to push interfaces more towards tablet/smartphone UI's. IMO, it's somewhat more prevalent in less complicated software, e.g. web browsers; you won't find it nearly so much in, say, programming tools such as IDEs. It is also noteworthy that in a lot of software it actually IS there, but it's hidden fairly well. Whether or not they plan to remove it entirely eventually or leave it in as a subtle "advanced UI," I couldn't say, although it wouldn't surprise me if they push to eliminate it more in the future.

I don't run Thunderbird, but it's possible or probable it got hit with the same "remake the interface to look like Chrome" movement that ran over Firefox's UI. In that case they didn't quite remove the menu bar, but hid it (and most advanced commands) pretty darned well. Try using the alt key to bring it up, or try Alt-F to get into it, and you might be pleasantly surprised. Furthermore there might be an option to show it at all times, but remember to use the keyboard in it anyway. Stupid as it is, at least for Firefox, it shows more options in the dropdown menu if you activate the menu with a keyboard shortcut instead of using the mouse.
